families.title: Prime bags
families.mathematics: A number card splits into two whole numbers greater than 1 that multiply to it, until every card is prime; every route of a number ends in the same bag of primes (unique factorization). Choosing some tokens of a bag makes a value, and the values are exactly the divisors of the bag’s value, because the tokens left behind make the quotient and tokens with the same number are the same; a bag with e₁, …, e_r copies of its primes makes (e₁ + 1)⋯(e_r + 1) values. The least number with a given count of divisors puts the largest counts on the smallest primes: 6, 12, 24, 36, 48, 60 for 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12. The puzzles ask for every first split of a card, every value of a bag, and a bag with exactly k values, then the smallest one.
rules: A card splits into two whole numbers greater than 1 that multiply to it. A number that cannot split is prime; it becomes a round token.
Choose some tokens from a bag, each at most once. They multiply to a value; choosing none makes 1.
Tokens with the same number are the same: choosing a different one of them makes the same value.

parent.notice: Whether your child notices that adding a token keeps every value and adds new ones.
parent.prompt: When you add a 3, which new values can you make?
parent.explanation: Adding a token keeps every value the bag could already make, and the new values are old values times the new token. Taking a token out removes the values that needed it. The bag holds at most 7 tokens.
parent.extension: Build the smallest bags that make nine and ten values. (36 and 48.)
parent.connection: The divisors of n · p contain the divisors of n, and the new ones are p times divisors of n with one more copy of p.

rules: A card splits into two whole numbers greater than 1 that multiply to it. A number that cannot split is prime; it becomes a round token.

puzzles.idea: Choosing none makes 1 and choosing all makes the bag’s value; each token is in or out, so two different tokens make four values.
puzzles.prerequisites: Read numbers to 10 and tap; the app multiplies. No reading needed once a grown-up has read the goal line.
hints: Tap tokens to choose them, then Keep the value.
What value do you make if you choose no tokens at all?
Each token is chosen or not. Try every way.

parent.notice: Whether your child keeps 1 (nothing chosen) and 6 (everything chosen) without being told.
parent.explanation: The values are 1, 2, 3 and 6: each token is in or out, 2 × 2 = 4 ways, and each makes a different value. They are exactly the numbers that divide 6, because the tokens left behind always multiply to 6 divided by the value chosen. Choosing nothing makes 1, the number that changes nothing when you multiply by it.
parent.extension: Which numbers divide 6 with nothing left over? Compare them with the tray.
parent.connection: The values of a bag are the divisors of its value; the empty product is 1.

puzzles.provenance: New instance, after the choosing rules and worked example shared by both Week 96 packets (the 2, 2, 5 bag, choosing 2 and 5 to make 10).

parent.notice: Whether your child expects another 2 to make a new value, and what they say when Keep stays off and the tray rings the value they already have.
parent.prompt: Puzzle 1 had two tokens and this bag has three. Why do they make the same number of values?
parent.explanation: 1, 2, 4 and 8. Choosing the first 2 or the third makes the same value, so what counts is how many 2s: none, one, two or three, four values. Three different tokens (puzzle 7) make eight.
parent.extension: How many values would five 2s make? (Six: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32.)
parent.connection: A prime power pᵉ has e + 1 divisors: 1, p, …, pᵉ.

puzzles.title: Split 12
puzzles.objective: Split the card into two numbers that multiply to it, and keep splitting until every card is prime. Start a different way each run. Press That’s all when every first split is on the shelf.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Start the split every way you can, and split to the end each time.
puzzles.instruction: Split the card into two numbers that multiply to it, and keep splitting until every card is prime. Start a different way each run. Press That’s all when every first split is on the shelf.
puzzles.controls: The chosen card is ringed; tap another card to choose it. Tap a key to split the card: 4 splits 20 into 4 × 5. New run starts the card again. Press That’s all when every first split is on the shelf. Undo takes back the last move.
rules: A card splits into two whole numbers greater than 1 that multiply to it. A number that cannot split is prime; it becomes a round token.
Choose some tokens from a bag, each at most once. They multiply to a value; choosing none makes 1.
Tokens with the same number are the same: choosing a different one of them makes the same value.
That’s all says whether a first split is missing.
puzzles.idea: Different first splits of 12 finish in the same bag of primes.
puzzles.prerequisites: Multiplication facts to 10 × 10, or trying keys one at a time (a wrong key is refused). Equal rows of counters help.
hints: Tap a key that makes 12 when you multiply it by something. Keep splitting until every card is a round token.
12 is 2 rows of 6. Is it some other number of equal rows too?
Press New run and try a different key first.

parent.notice: Whether your child is surprised that the second route ends in the same tokens.
parent.prompt: Could a different start ever end with different tokens?
parent.explanation: 12 splits first as 2 × 6 or 3 × 4 (6 × 2 and 4 × 3 are the same splits). Then 6 becomes 2 × 3, or 4 becomes 2 × 2, and both routes finish with 2, 2, 3. Every route of every number finishes in one bag: unique factorization. Two routes are evidence, not proof; the proof through the fact that a prime dividing a product divides one of its factors is on p. 6 of the Week 96 guide.
parent.extension: Make 12 counters into rectangles: 2 rows of 6 and 3 rows of 4 are the first splits.
parent.connection: Unique factorization of whole numbers (the fundamental theorem of arithmetic).

puzzles.provenance: Week 96 grades 2–3 Problem 1 (card 12, two splitting routes), as a find-every: every first split.

Choose the 3 or leave it out; with each, choose no 2s, one or two.

parent.notice: Whether your child works in an order (everything with the 3, everything without) or at random.
parent.prompt: Is every number that divides 12 in your tray?
parent.explanation: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12, every divisor of 12. Without the 3 there are 1, 2 and 4; with it, 3, 6 and 12: no, one or two 2s each time, 3 × 2 = 6. A value chosen and the tokens left behind multiply to 12, so every value divides 12, and every divisor of 12 has its own tokens in the bag.
parent.extension: Pair each value with the tokens left behind: 1 with 12, 2 with 6, 3 with 4.
parent.connection: The divisors of a number are the sub-bags of its prime factorization.

parent.notice: Whether your child finds 6 × 6, and whether they keep splitting to the end each run.
parent.prompt: Why does every route end with the same four tokens?
parent.explanation: 2 × 18, 3 × 12, 4 × 9 and 6 × 6 (9 × 4 is 4 × 9 again). Every route finishes with 2, 2, 3, 3. With 1 × 36, the splits pair up the divisors of 36: 1 with 36, 2 with 18, 3 with 12, 4 with 9, and 6 with itself, which is why 36 has an odd number of divisors.
parent.extension: Count the values of the bag 2, 2, 3, 3 (puzzle 10). How do they match these splits?
parent.connection: A first split is a divisor d with d ≤ n ÷ d; a square has one split of a number by itself.

puzzles.provenance: Week 96 Problem 1 (card 36, in both packets), as a find-every: every first split.

puzzles.controls: Tap 2, 3, 5 or 7 to put a token in the bag, and − under it to take one out. Tap tokens in the bag to choose them; Keep puts their value in the tray. Press That’s all when every value is kept. Undo takes back the last move.

puzzles.idea: A bag’s count of values comes from how many copies of each prime it has: two of one and one of another make six.
puzzles.prerequisites: Multiplication with the app’s help, and planning a bag from earlier puzzles, perhaps by trying and adjusting.
hints: Put tokens in the bag, keep every value it makes, and press That’s all.
Puzzles 4 and 5 had bags that made this many values.
Try two of one number and one of another.

parent.notice: Whether your child reuses a bag from puzzle 4 or 5, or builds and tests new ones.
parent.prompt: Which other bags make six values?
parent.explanation: Two copies of one prime and one of another make 3 × 2 = 6 values (12, 18, 20, 28, 45, 50, …), and so do five copies of one prime (32 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2). No other bag does, because 6 is only 3 × 2 or 6. Any of these 16 bags solves it.
parent.extension: What is the smallest bag that makes six values? (12.)
parent.connection: τ(n) = 6 exactly for n = p²q or p⁵.

puzzles.provenance: Week 96 grades 2–3 Problem 4 (build a bag that makes exactly 4, 6 and 8 values), the six.

parent.prompt: How do you know you have every first split?
parent.explanation: 2 × 30, 3 × 20, 4 × 15, 5 × 12 and 6 × 10: the keys that divide 60 are 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6, and every split has a part of 7 or less because 8 × 8 is more than 60. Every route finishes with 2, 2, 3, 5.

parent.connection: Divisor pairs d · (n ÷ d) with d < √n: a non-square n has τ(n) ÷ 2 of them, one of them 1 × n.

puzzles.controls: Tap 2, 3, 5 or 7 to put a token in the bag, and − under it to take one out. Tap tokens in the bag to choose them; Keep puts their value in the tray. Press That’s all when every value is kept. Undo takes back the last move.
rules: A card splits into two whole numbers greater than 1 that multiply to it. A number that cannot split is prime; it becomes a round token.

Tokens with the same number are the same: choosing a different one of them makes the same value.

puzzles.idea: Put the extra copies on the smallest prime: three 2s and a 3 (24) beat 2, 3, 5 (30).
puzzles.prerequisites: Fluent multiplication; comparing bags that make the same count, and the idea that a count of values comes from how many copies of each prime the bag has.
hints: Build a bag that makes exactly eight values, keep them all, and press That’s all.
Puzzles 6 and 7 both made eight values. Which bag was smaller?
Three copies of one prime and one of another make eight too.

parent.notice: Whether your child compares 24 and 30 from puzzles 6 and 7, or builds from scratch.
parent.prompt: How do you know no smaller bag makes eight values?
parent.explanation: Eight values come from three different primes (2 × 2 × 2), three of one prime and one of another (4 × 2), or seven of one (8). The smallest bag of each kind is 2 · 3 · 5 = 30, 2 · 2 · 2 · 3 = 24 and 2⁷ = 128, so 24. Checking every number below 24 confirms it.

parent.connection: The least number with a given divisor count uses the smallest primes with exponents in decreasing order.

puzzles.title: Smallest with twelve
puzzles.objective: Build the smallest bag that makes exactly 12 values. Keep every value it makes, then press That’s all.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Build the smallest bag that makes exactly 12 values, and keep them all.
puzzles.instruction: Build the smallest bag that makes exactly 12 values. Keep every value it makes, then press That’s all.
puzzles.controls: Tap 2, 3, 5 or 7 to put a token in the bag, and − under it to take one out. Tap tokens in the bag to choose them; Keep puts their value in the tray. Press That’s all when every value is kept. Undo takes back the last move.
rules: A card splits into two whole numbers greater than 1 that multiply to it. A number that cannot split is prime; it becomes a round token.
Choose some tokens from a bag, each at most once. They multiply to a value; choosing none makes 1.
Tokens with the same number are the same: choosing a different one of them makes the same value.
That’s all says whether a value is missing.
Kept values stay while the bag can still make them.
puzzles.idea: Twelve is 3 × 2 × 2, 4 × 3, 6 × 2 or 12: compare the smallest bag of each pattern.
puzzles.prerequisites: Fluent multiplication; comparing bags that make the same count, and the idea that a count of values comes from how many copies of each prime the bag has.
hints: Build a bag that makes exactly twelve values, keep them all, and press That’s all.
Puzzle 11’s bag made twelve values. Is there a smaller one?
Twelve is 3 × 2 × 2: two of one prime, one each of two others.

parent.notice: Whether your child tries 72 (puzzle 11’s extension) before 60, and why they move on.
parent.prompt: Why can’t a bag smaller than 60 make twelve values?
parent.explanation: The patterns are two copies of one prime and one each of two others (smallest 2 · 2 · 3 · 5 = 60), three and two (2 · 2 · 2 · 3 · 3 = 72), five and one (2⁵ · 3 = 96), and eleven of one (2¹¹, more tokens than the bag holds). So 60, and every number below 60 has a different count.
parent.extension: Find the smallest bags with nine and ten values. (36 and 48.)
parent.connection: Highly composite numbers: 60 has more divisors than any smaller number.
